questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the following are stochastic vectors?

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 0 \\ 0.5\end{aligned}],\,v=[\begin{aligned}-0.45 \\ 1.55\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our vectors in turn.

- Vector $u$ is a stochastic vector. Indeed, 

- its entries are all nonnegative, and

- the entries add up to one:

$$
0.5+0+0.5=1
$$

- Vector $v$ is *not* a stochastic vector since it contains negative entries.

- Vector $w$ is *not* a stochastic vector since the entries do not add up to one:

$$
0+0=0\ne 1
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$u$ only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0 & 0.9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.9 & 0 & 0.1\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 \\ 1.1 & 0.8\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $U$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its second column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0 & 0.9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.9 & 0 & 0.1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $V$  is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.2 \\ 1.1 & 0.8\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $W$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are non-negative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0.7\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.5+0.5=1 \\ 0.3+0.7=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$W$ only."

questions.problem:
There are three cable TV providers in a particular apartment block: provider $A,$ provider $B,$ and provider $C.$ A study has shown that, each year

- from the tenants using provider $A,$ $80%$ swap to provider $B$ and $10%$ swap to provider $C,$

- from the tenants using provider $B,$ $25%$ swap to provider $A$ and $25%$ swap to provider $C,$

- from the tenants using provider $C,$ $70%$ swap to provider $A$ and $10%$ swap to provider $B.$

The stochastic matrix that describes this situation is given below. What is the value of $a+b+c?$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & a & 0.7 \\ 0.8 & 0.5 & b \\ c & 0.25 & 0.2\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the following situation for each year:

- From the tenants using provider $A,$ $80%$ swap to provider $B$ and $10%$ swap to provider $C.$  This implies that $10%$ of them continue using provider $A.$

- From the tenants using provider $B,$ $25%$ swap to provider $A$ and $25%$ swap to provider $C.$ This implies that $50%$ of them continue using provider $B.$

- From the tenants using provider $C,$ $70%$ swap to provider $A$ and $10%$ swap to provider $B.$ This implies that $20%$ of them continue using provider $C.$

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Provider A** | **Provider B** | **Provider C** |
| To: | **Provider A** | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.7$ |
| **Provider B** | $0.8$ | $0.5$ | $0.1$ |  |
| **Provider C** | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.2$ |  |

We can write the corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.25 & 0.7 \\ 0.8 & 0.5 & 0.1 \\ 0.1 & 0.25 & 0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we have

$$
a+b+c=0.25+0.1+0.1=0.45.
$$

- On a day that follows a rainy day, there is a $40%$ chance not to have precipitation and a $5%$ chance to have snow. This implies a $55%$ chance of having rain on this day.

- On a day that follows a snowy day, there is a $50%$ chance not to have precipitation and a $5%$ chance to have rain. This implies a $45%$ chance of having snow on this day.

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a State Vector
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.9 & 0.8\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0.3 \\ 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider a Markov chain with the stochastic matrix $P$ and the initial state vector ${x}_{0}$ given above. Calculate the state vector ${x}_{1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the state vector ${x}_{1},$ we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.9 & 0.8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.3 \\ 0.7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.17 \\ 0.83\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.85 \\ 0.75 & 0.15\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0.4 \\ 0.6\end{aligned}]
$$

 
Consider a Markov chain with the stochastic matrix $P$ and the initial state vector ${x}_{0}$ given above. Calculate the state vector ${x}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the state vector ${x}_{2},$ we apply two steps of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0},\,{x}_{2}=P{x}_{1}
$$

After the first step, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.85 \\ 0.75 & 0.15\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.4 \\ 0.6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.61 \\ 0.39\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, after the second step, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.85 \\ 0.75 & 0.15\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.61 \\ 0.39\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.484 \\ 0.516\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix and Making a Prediction
questions.problem:
A certain company produces two types of smartphones: Phone $A$ and Phone $B.$ The following table describes how the number of customers changes between both types of smartphones each year:

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Phone $A$** | **Phone $B$** |
| To: | **Phone $A$** | $0.6$ | $0.3$ |
| **Phone $B$** | $0.4$ | $0.7$ |  |

That is, $40%$ of Phone $A$ customers switch to Phone $B$ each year, and $30%$ of Phone $B$ customers switch to Phone $A.$

Currently, $600\,000$ customers use Phone $A,$ while $400\,000$ customers use Phone $B.$ How many customers will use Phone $A$ in one year? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.6 & 0.3 \\ 0.4 & 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each smartphone is

$$
[\begin{aligned}600\,000 \\ 400\,000\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{1\,000\,000}[\begin{aligned}600\,000 \\ 400\,000\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.6 \\ 0.4\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.6 & 0.3 \\ 0.4 & 0.7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.6 \\ 0.4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.48 \\ 0.52\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one year, $48%$ of customers will use Phone $A.$ Computing $48%$ of $1\,000\,000,$ we obtain

$$
1\,000\,000\cdot 0.48=480\,000.
$$

Therefore, $480\,000$ customers will use Phone $A$ in one year.

A certain cinema sells three types of popcorn: traditional, butter, and caramelized. The following table describes how the number of customers changes between the three types of popcorn each month:

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| To: | **Traditional** | $0.4$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| **Butter** | $0.3$ | $0.5$ | $0.2$ |  |
| **Caramelized** | $0.3$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ |  |

For example, $30%$ of traditional popcorn customers switch to butter popcorn each month, and $40%$ of butter popcorn customers switch to caramelized popcorn.

Currently, $400$ customers buy traditional popcorn, $300$ customers buy butter popcorn, and $300$ customers buy caramelized popcorn. How many customers will purchase butter popcorn in one month? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of popcorn customers is

$$
[\begin{aligned}400 \\ 300 \\ 300\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{1\,000}[\begin{aligned}400 \\ 300 \\ 300\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.4 \\ 0.3 \\ 0.3\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.4 \\ 0.3 \\ 0.3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.25 \\ 0.33 \\ 0.42\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one year, $33%$ of customers will buy butter popcorn. Computing $33%$ of $1\,000,$ we obtain

$$
1\,000\cdot 0.33=330.
$$

Therefore, $330$ customers will buy butter popcorn in one month.

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.2 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.4\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of ground coffee is

$$
[\begin{aligned}300\,000 \\ 500\,000 \\ 200\,000\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{1\,000\,000}[\begin{aligned}300\,000 \\ 500\,000 \\ 200\,000\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.3 \\ 0.5 \\ 0.2\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.2 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.3 \\ 0.5 \\ 0.2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.29 \\ 0.47 \\ 0.24\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

1\,000\,000\cdot 0.29=290\,000.

questions.problem:
A certain company produces three types of milk: whole, skim, and lactose-free. The following table describes how the number of customers changes between the three types of milk each year:

|  |  | From: |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Whole** | **Skim** | **Lactose-free** |
| To: | **Whole** | $0.5$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ |
| **Skim** | $0.3$ | $0.4$ | $0.4$ |  |
| **Lactose-free** | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |  |

For example, $30%$ of whole milk customers switch to skim milk each year, and $20%$ of lactose-free milk customers switch to whole milk.

Currently, $400\,000$ customers consume whole milk, $400\,000$ customers consume skim milk, and $200\,000$ customers consume lactose-free milk. How many customers will consume whole milk after one year? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.4\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of milk is

$$
[\begin{aligned}400\,000 \\ 400\,000 \\ 200\,000\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{1\,000\,000}[\begin{aligned}400\,000 \\ 400\,000 \\ 200\,000\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.4 \\ 0.4 \\ 0.2\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.4 \\ 0.4 \\ 0.2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.36 \\ 0.36 \\ 0.28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one year, $36%$ of customers will consume whole milk. Computing $36%$ of $1\,000\,000,$ we obtain

$$
1\,000\,000\cdot 0.36=360\,000.
$$

Therefore, $360\,000$ customers will consume whole milk after one year.

questions.problem:
A certain company produces two types of motorcycles: classic and high-cylinder. The following table describes how the number of customers changes between both types of motorcycles each decade:

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Classic** | **High-Cylinder** |
| To: | **Classic** | $0.6$ | $0.2$ |
| **High-Cylinder** | $0.4$ | $0.8$ |  |

That is, $40%$ of classic motorcycle customers switch to high-cylinder each decade, and $20%$ of high-cylinder motorcycle customers switch to Classic.

Currently, $7\,000$ customers use classic motorcycles while $3\,000$ customers use high-cylinder motorcycles. How many customers will use high-cylinder motorcycles in one decade? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.4 & 0.8\end{aligned}]
$$

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of motorcycle is

$$
[\begin{aligned}7\,000 \\ 3\,000\end{aligned}].
$$

Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(10\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

$$
{x}_{0}=\frac{1}{10\,000}[\begin{aligned}7\,000 \\ 3\,000\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.7 \\ 0.3\end{aligned}]
$$

To find the state vector ${x}_{1}$ after one decade, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
{x}_{1}=P{x}_{0}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.4 & 0.8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.7 \\ 0.3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.48 \\ 0.52\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one decade, $52%$ of customers will use high-cylinder motorcycles. Computing $52%$ of $10\,000,$ we obtain

$$
10\,000\cdot 0.52=5\,200.
$$

Therefore, $5\,200$ customers will use high-cylinder motorcycles in one decade.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14059948/assets/70ee929c71d89a443d3ea0efc39ed225f344685059b86a04285a118a476da0f8.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix $\bf{U}$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0 \\ 1.2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- Matrix $\bf{V}$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.95 \\ 0.65 & 0.05\end{aligned}]\,\begin{aligned}0.35+0.65=1 \\ 0.95+0.05=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- Matrix $\bf{W}$ is *not* a stochastic matrix since its third column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.4 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.7\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\bf{V}$ only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix Given Some Data
canonical_examples.problem:
There are two groups of people in a particular city: those who use their own vehicles and those who use public transport. A study has shown that, each year

- $35\%$ of people who used their own vehicles swap to public transport, and

- $25\%$ of people who used public transport swap to their own vehicles.

Give the stochastic matrix that describes how people change their means of transportation each year.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are given the following situation for each year: 

- $35\%$ of people who used their own vehicles swap to public transport. This implies that $65\%$ of them remain using their own vehicles.

- $25\%$ of people who used public transport swap to their own vehicles. This implies that $75\%$ of them remain using public transport.

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Vehicles** | **Public Transport ** |
| To: | **Vehicles** | $0.65$ | $0.25$ |
| **Public Transport** | $0.35$ | $0.75$ |  |

Note that we can write a corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14059948/assets/b21fee1abe56dcfdc687be14278c62a20d201ff00e96f1e5918ce22d9dc8b03c.png)

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14059948/assets/165917feacd28344502759fc6e03f96c5b54d9530701916b746fc489374a6d0b.png) 

Consider a Markov chain with the stochastic matrix $P$ and the initial state vector $\mathbf{x}_0$ given above. Calculate the state vector $\mathbf{x}_2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_2,$ we apply two steps of the Markov chain:

$$
\mathbf{x_1}=P\mathbf{x}_0, \qquad \mathbf{x}_2=P\mathbf{x}_1
$$

After the first step, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.1 \\ 0.5 & 0.9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 0.8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.18 \\ 0.82\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, after the second step, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.5 & 0.1 \\ 0.5 & 0.9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.18 \\ 0.82\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.172 \\ 0.828\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A certain industry produces $2$ types of sugar, namely sugar $A$ and sugar $B$. The following table describes how the number of consumers changes between both types of sugar in a month:

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Sugar $A$** | **Sugar $B$** |
| To: | **Sugar $A$** | $0.3$ | $0.45$ |
| **Sugar $B$** | $0.7$ | $0.55$ |  |

That is, $70\%$ of sugar $A$ customers switch to sugar $B$ each month, and $45\%$ of sugar $B$ customers switch to sugar $A.$

Currently, $600$ customers use sugar $A,$ while $400$ customers use sugar $B.$ How many customers will use sugar $A$ in one month? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14059948/assets/451b82e8cb00ede7b0ddf73f35c0555d0eeeeefc5beb5ce4fddd54f0df5f2577.png)

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of sugar is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14059948/assets/56952aeed1d718033af8a3e6d09e8e269f1d70aa8dc31609b8289f025f2e6bd6.png)
Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14059948/assets/cae1bed6b8b01b3ff66c2e8bacf7a10f6c0ece53f3aeac0fb1a51e8fc3c07e8e.png)

To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ after one month, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

$$
\mathbf{x}_1=P\mathbf{x}_0
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.45 \\ 0.7 & 0.55\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.6 \\ 0.4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.36 \\ 0.64\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, after one month, $\color{blue}36\%$ of customers will use sugar $A.$ Computing $36\%$ of $1\,000,$ we obtain

$$
1\,000 \cdot 0.36 = 360.
$$

Therefore, $360$ customers will use sugar $A$ in one month.
